# True or false: Operating model

Who decides, who is consulted and how teams are shaped set the speed of everything else. These statements test the beliefs that slow organisations down.

10 statements (Foundation 4, Standard 5, Assured 1). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area operating-model`.

### 1. An important decision can have two accountable people, so that both departments are represented.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Every decision has exactly one accountable person and a time limit. With two, each waits for the other and nobody owns the result. Pick one; the other becomes consulted.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/decision-rights.md](../../playbook/operating-model/decision-rights.md)

</details>

### 2. Being consulted on a decision gives you a veto over it.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Consulted people give their input by a deadline. The accountable person then decides. Treating consulted as a veto turns every decision into a negotiation with no end date.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/decision-rights.md](../../playbook/operating-model/decision-rights.md)

</details>

### 3. Decisions should be made at the lowest level that has the information and will live with the result.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The people closest to the work usually know the most and bear the consequences. Escalate only when a decision crosses team boundaries, cannot be undone cheaply, or breaks an agreed standard. Otherwise everything queues for the CTO.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/decision-rights.md](../../playbook/operating-model/decision-rights.md)

</details>

### 4. Strong engineering governance means every significant change queues for a review board.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Govern with written standards, automated checks and a small review group that answers within a fixed time. Review only the decisions that are hard to reverse or cross team boundaries. Everything else uses the advice process.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/engineering-governance.md](../../playbook/operating-model/engineering-governance.md)

</details>

### 5. Every exception to an engineering standard should be written down, owned and given an expiry date.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Waivers that never expire quietly become the real standard. An owner and an expiry date force a decision: fix the gap, renew the exception on purpose, or change the standard. A monthly report of expiring waivers keeps this cheap.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/engineering-governance.md](../../playbook/operating-model/engineering-governance.md)

</details>

### 6. For a single product, separate front end, back end and database teams are the most efficient structure.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Component teams turn every feature into a hand-off between teams. Organise most engineers into stream-aligned teams that own a product or service end to end. Keep specialists as enabling or complicated-subsystem teams.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/team-topology.md](../../playbook/operating-model/team-topology.md)

</details>

### 7. Team Topologies describes four team types: stream-aligned, enabling, complicated-subsystem and platform.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Skelton and Pais (2019) describe these four types and three ways teams interact: collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating. Most engineers belong in stream-aligned teams. Add the other types only when they reduce load on those teams.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/team-topology.md](../../playbook/operating-model/team-topology.md)

</details>

### 8. When two teams collaborate well, they should stay in collaboration mode permanently.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Collaboration is expensive: it uses both teams' attention and blurs who owns what. Use it for a set period to discover the right interface. Then set an end date, write the interface down and move to X-as-a-Service.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/team-topology.md](../../playbook/operating-model/team-topology.md)

</details>

### 9. A detailed 40-page technology pack gives a board better oversight than a two-page summary.

Level: Assured

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Long packs arrive late and bury what the board needs to act on. The playbook recommends two pages with 8 to 12 measures, showing trends and thresholds. Board members can then see quickly which numbers are outside the agreed risk appetite.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/it-governance.md](../../playbook/operating-model/it-governance.md)

</details>

### 10. An organisation can adopt ITIL 4 without adding change approval meetings.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** ITIL 4 describes a service value system, not a meeting schedule. Copying it as a set of approval meetings can add a week to every change. Use pre-authorised standard changes and evidence that the pipeline produces automatically.

Read more: [playbook/operating-model/it-governance.md](../../playbook/operating-model/it-governance.md)

</details>
